title: Prior Authorization in 2027: The API Can Move the Information, But Someone Still Has to Own the Work
summary: Prior authorization APIs can improve information flow in 2027, but hospitals still need clear cross-functional ownership, strong UM handoffs, and defined automation and exception workflows.
body_markdown:
Prior authorization has always been more than a payer requirement. It is an operational workflow.


That distinction is going to matter even more in 2027.


Beginning January 1, 2027, CMS requires impacted payers to implement Prior Authorization APIs that can help providers determine whether prior authorization is required, identify documentation requirements, submit authorization requests, and receive responses electronically. Those responses can include an approval, a specific denial reason, or a request for additional information.


That has the potential to eliminate a lot of manual work. But an API can only move the information. **Someone still has to own what happens next.**


## One of the Biggest Problems Happens Before the Authorization Is Submitted


From my experience, one of the most common breakdowns in prior authorization starts with something very basic: **Do we know what the payer requires for this specific service?**


Organizations may have teams checking portals, payer reference tools, internal grids, or other sources to determine whether authorization is required and what documentation is needed. The new API functionality has the potential to make that information much easier to identify electronically.


That is a meaningful improvement. But knowing the requirement is only the first step. The organization still needs a workflow that ensures the authorization is obtained timely and that every team involved understands its responsibility.


## Prior Authorization Should Not Become a Back-End Revenue Cycle Problem


One of the operational mistakes I have seen is allowing responsibility for prior authorization failures to fall too heavily on Patient Financial Services. A claim denies for no authorization or an authorization mismatch, and suddenly the billing team is expected to figure out why it happened, who missed the step, and how to fix it.


By then, the workflow has already failed.


**Prior authorization should be designed as an upfront operational process, not a back-end Revenue Cycle cleanup process.**


Patient Financial Services should provide feedback when authorization-related denials or payment issues occur. That information is important for identifying trends and improving the process. But the PFS or billing director should not be responsible for making sure every upstream department performs its role correctly.


**If we are waiting until Patient Financial Services receives a denial to figure out who should have owned the authorization, we identified the responsibility too late.**


## Prior Authorization Governance Should Be Cross-Functional


I do not think ownership belongs exclusively to Patient Access, Utilization Management, Managed Care, or IT. The process crosses all of them.


In larger Revenue Cycle organizations, there is often a VP or other senior leader with oversight across Patient Access, Utilization Management, and at least some components of Revenue Cycle technology. Even when IT or Managed Care sits outside that leader’s direct reporting structure, those teams usually need to be close partners.


That type of cross-functional ownership makes sense for prior authorization. The executive owner does not have to perform the work. The role is to make sure the overall authorization process is coordinated and that each area knows where its responsibility begins and ends.


IT can support the build, integration, alerts, work queues, and API connections. Managed Care can assist with payer policy, contract interpretation, and higher-level payer escalation. Patient Access and authorization teams can perform much of the front-end work. Utilization Management plays an especially important role when the patient’s clinical course changes.


## UM Owns the Trigger When the Clinical Plan Changes


Obtaining the initial authorization does not mean the process is finished. The procedure can change. The level of care can change. The length of stay can extend. Additional services can be ordered. The treatment plan can evolve.


When that happens, the original authorization may no longer match the care being delivered. In many situations, the team responsible for submitting an authorization would have no way of knowing that the clinical plan changed unless someone tells them.


That is why I believe **Utilization Management should own identifying when a clinical change may require the authorization to be reviewed or updated** , even if another team is ultimately responsible for submitting the reauthorization or amendment.


UM is close enough to the clinical progression of the patient to recognize that something has changed. Then the workflow should clearly define what happens next: UM triggers the process, the responsible authorization team takes the appropriate action, the status is updated, and the information is visible to everyone who needs it.


## This Is Where the API Could Be Especially Valuable


The API has the potential to improve several of these handoffs. If payer requirements are available electronically, teams may be able to identify earlier whether authorization is required and what documentation is needed.


If the payer requests additional information, that response can be returned electronically. If the payer denies the request, the response can include a specific reason. That creates an opportunity to build much more connected workflows.


For example, a payer response requests additional documentation. The authorization team receives the response. UM is involved if the missing information is clinical. The appropriate team supplies the documentation. The request is resubmitted or updated. And the status remains visible through the process.


**The API can improve the handoff. It cannot define the ownership.**


## Automation Can Help With the Work, but It Does Not Eliminate Accountability


There is also an opportunity for organizations to use automation or outside support for portions of the authorization process.


Routine verification, payer requirement checks, status monitoring, and response tracking may be good candidates for automation or external support. That can reduce manual touches and create additional capacity.


Clinical changes, unclear payer requirements, denials, and exception handling should have a clearly defined path back to the appropriate internal team.


**The work can be automated or delegated. The accountability cannot.** The more of the process that becomes automated, the more important it is to define which steps can run independently and which ones need human review.


## What Revenue Cycle Leaders Should Validate Now


The most useful preparation is not another generic readiness checklist. It is validating whether the authorization operating model actually works.


- Do we have a current, reliable source for payer-specific authorization requirements?
- Is there a named owner for every major step and handoff in the authorization process?
- Does UM know when it must trigger a review or reauthorization because the clinical plan changed?
- Are payer responses routed to the right team quickly enough for someone to act?
- Are automation, vendor-supported tasks, human-review points, and escalation rules clearly defined?


## Do Not Start With the Technology


If I were advising an organization preparing for 2027, I would not start by asking whether the API connection is ready. I would start with the people who will actually use the information.


The change needs to be communicated broadly to every impacted area. Then the organization should review the current authorization process from beginning to end: plot the workflow, identify the owners, document the handoffs, identify where UM needs to trigger action, define what happens when the payer asks for more information, define what happens when care changes, and define the escalation path.


Then look at how the API changes or improves each of those steps.


If the workflow is solid before the technology is layered in, the API can strengthen the process. If the workflow is unclear, the API may simply make the gaps move faster.


## The API Is an Opportunity to Fix the Process, Not Just Digitize It


The 2027 prior authorization requirements are understandably being discussed as an interoperability and technology initiative. They are. But for Revenue Cycle leaders, they are also an opportunity to revisit how authorization work is actually being managed.


The goal should not simply be to replace a portal search or payer call with an API transaction. The bigger opportunity is to create a process where everyone involved knows what the payer requires, what they personally own, what happens when something changes, and where the work goes next.


**The organizations that benefit most from the 2027 API changes will not be the ones that simply connect the technology. They will be the ones that use it to reinforce a clear operating model for prior authorization.**


**The API can move the information. Accountability still has to be designed.**
